searches.note: Twenty four searches of a share of twenty eight, four left unspent, none of them the author's. Twelve were restricted to a house's own domain (ridgewine.com four times, calerawine.com twice, aubonclimat.com once, tablascreek.com three times, bonnydoonvineyard.com twice) and are read as primary through their summaries; eleven kept the house's own domain out, and where the author had leant on them Wikipedia, Decanter, Vinous, BenitoLink, Wine and Spirits Magazine, the Wine History Project and Vinetur, so that the second source would be independent; one went to the open web. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The making, the blend and the sites went first to the house's own domain, read through its search summaries; the history went to the open web with the house's domain and the author's secondary sources kept out, so that each date found its second source elsewhere.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was found in no source of this check it was cut or said with less. A distractor that the house's own account made half true was replaced, so that each question has one right answer.

The dead are named with their dates where two sources agree (Josh Jensen, Jim Clendenen, Robert Haas); the doctor of Monte Bello, the theologian of 1949, the engineers of 1959 and every living person stay described.

Sources whose title or address names a living person (a winemaker's essay on ingredient labels, a sale notice, a columnist's site, a critic's site, a magazine interview) were met among the results and are cited neither in the fragment nor here. The serving temperatures (16 to 18 for Monte Bello and the Esprit, 15 to 17 for the two Pinots and the Cigare) agree with the service reference and with the Pinot Noir records of Burgundy and Sonoma.

tested: The doctor's purchase of 1886 and the first vintage of 1892: Ridge's history, timeline and Historic Monte Bello give 1885 for the purchase of about 180 acres and the winery completed and bonded in time for the 1892 vintage; SevenFifty Daily and VinePair agree. Changed to 1885.

The winery the engineers bonded in 1962: Ridge's history says the theologian bought the abandoned winery and vineyard just below the doctor's in the 1940s, and the engineers re-bonded the winery for the 1962 vintage; SevenFifty Daily and VinePair give the purchase of the doctor's own winery in 1968. Changed.
The replanting of 1949: the timeline gives 1949 and the history the late 1940s; the oldest vines are Short's of 1949. Confirmed.
The founders of 1959: three or four engineers from the Stanford Research Institute by different Ridge pages. A small group kept.
The winemaker of 1969 to 2016: joined in 1969 (VinePair, SevenFifty Daily, Ridge), retirement announced in 2016 (The Underground Wine Letter, July 2016), chairman later. Confirmed.

The sale of 1986: Ridge's history gives the last day of 1986, a subsidiary of Otsuka America, and the buyer's promise to leave the business alone; its report of 2024 names Otsuka Pharmaceutical; The Underground Wine Letter and Yahoo News agree on 1986. Confirmed and retold.
The sites: 1300 to 2760 feet on the recent sheets, fractured limestone under decomposing Franciscan greenstone with clay and loam. About 400 to over 800 metres confirmed; the thin layer is cut.
The making: native yeasts and a natural malolactic on Ridge's sheets, air dried American oak 90 to 95 per cent with a little French; the malolactic's vessel not given. Retold without it.
The ingredient label: Ridge's own account of its label gives the 2011 vintage. Dated.
The Paris placings of 1976 and 2006: the library and Wikipedia; not searched again.
The cards and the questions: one right answer each; the Japanese group card is retold to Ridge's own account. Sound.
The rules: nobody living named (the winemaker of 1969 is described), no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash. Sound.

changed.was: Prohibition and neglect left the vineyard all but abandoned by the 1940s, and in 1949 a small block of Cabernet Sauvignon was replanted there; their grapes would make the first Ridge wines. In 1959 a small group of engineers from the Stanford Research Institute bought land on the ridge, and in 1962 they bonded the old winery as Ridge Vineyards and made the first commercial Monte Bello.
changed.now: By the 1940s his winery had closed and its vines were abandoned. In 1949 a theologian who had bought an old winery and vineyard just below replanted Cabernet Sauvignon there, and those vines would make the first Ridge wines. In 1959 a small group of engineers from the Stanford Research Institute bought his land, and in 1962 they bonded its winery again as Ridge Vineyards and made the first commercial Monte Bello; in 1968 they bought the doctor's old winery as well.
changed.why: The engineers bonded the theologian's winery below the doctor's in 1962 and bought the doctor's winery only in 1968; the closing of the doctor's winery is 1943 on one Ridge page and after Prohibition on others.

tested: Josh Jensen's dates: born 11 February 1944 in Seattle (Wine Spectator), died 11 June 2022 at 78 (Wine Enthusiast, San Francisco Chronicle, The Drinks Business). Confirmed.

The find of 1974, the founding and planting of 1975, the first crop of 1978, Mount Harlan's appellation of 1990 and the sale to Duckhorn in 2017: Wine Spectator, Wine Industry Advisor, Wine Enthusiast and the house. Confirmed; Decanter's 1971 a slip.

The three parcels: Selleck and Reed five acres each and Jensen fourteen, by the house; Jensen named for the founder's father, Reed for an investor, Selleck for a mentor, by Duckhorn's tribute and its reprint. The largest stands; the founder's name becomes his father's.

Height and coolness: the house gives an average of 2,200 feet and cold marine air drawn in through Monterey Bay, 25 miles away on its sheets, 37 miles from the open Pacific in its history. The trap and the wine question are set right.
The kiln: restored in 1997 on the house's timeline alone; no quarry date and no masonry found. Hedged and trimmed.
The Viognier: two acres planted in 1983 and three more in 1989, among California's first, by the house; Tablas Creek's blog names Calera among the pioneers. Retold.

The making: whole clusters, native yeasts, open fermenters, punch downs, pressed after fourteen days at least, gravity flow, eighteen months in French oak, thirty per cent new, on the house's pages for 2019 and 2021; filtration said only of a Ryan sheet of 2002. Filtration cut.
The cards and the questions: the wine question had a half true option; both questions now have one right answer.
The rules: the founder dead and dated; nobody living named; no price, score or volatile fact; British; no dash. Sound.

tested: Robert Haas's dates: born in Brooklyn in 1927, died 18 March 2018 at 90 (Wine Spectator, The Drinks Business, Wine Enthusiast, San Francisco Chronicle). Confirmed; the tenth decade cut.
The purchase of 1989 with the Perrin family, the planting of 1994 and the winery's debut in 1997: Wine Spectator and the house. Confirmed.
The cuttings of 1990 and the quarantine: three years in two accounts, released in 1992 or 1993; a greenhouse of 1992 for propagation. Some three years kept.
The nursery's reach: cuttings to six hundred growers in one account, a million grafts in a decade in Wikipedia. The claim on much of the nation's Rhone vines is eased.

The names: Esprit de Beaucastel until the 2011 vintage, Esprit de Tablas from it, on the house's pages; the vertical of 2000 to 2023 on its blog; a Wine Advocate review of 2003 says the Grand Cuvee was renamed Esprit de Beaucastel. Worded as a name taken in 2000.
The blend: 49, 46 and 40 per cent Mourvedre for 2015 to 2017 with Grenache, Syrah and Counoise. Two fifths to a half.

The making: native yeasts in wooden uprights, open tanks and closed steel; blended in May for the 2015, a further year in foudres of 1,200 gallons, bottled in June. The malolactic in barrel and the June blending are cut or eased.
Esprit de Tablas Blanc: Roussanne led in every sheet read. Confirmed. Cotes de Tablas: not found.
The cards and the questions: one right answer each. Sound.
The rules: Haas dead and dated; the Perrin brothers and the Haas heirs not named; nothing volatile; British; no dash. Sound.

tested: The founding of 1983: the library and most accounts, Wine Spectator among them; 1981 and 1982 in single accounts. Kept.
The first Cigare of 1984 and its release in 1986: Wine Spectator and the merchants. Confirmed.
The order of 1954 against flying saucers: the house, Decanter and several accounts. Confirmed.
The screwcap: the 2000 Cigare in one account, 2001 in another; the cork's funeral of 2002 in one. The start of the 2000s kept.
The first vineyard: Pierce's disease in 1994 in one account, phylloxera in another. Given up kept.

The sale of 2020 and the founder's part after it: Decanter, the San Francisco Chronicle and Wine Industry Advisor give January 2020, winemaker and partner at first; a later column an adviser without a title; the house's sheet of 2023 still lists him. Retold as at first.

The blend and the vessels: Grenache led in 2016, 2017 and the current release, Mourvedre led in 2012 by the author's reading; the 2015 partly in demijohns with wine from wooden uprights of 10,000 litres and puncheons; a later release in steel, bottled ten months after the harvest; Central Coast on the label. The making tied to its vintages.
Le Cigare Blanc: Grenache Blanc the larger share from 2011 to 2017, the 2017 the last with Roussanne. Set right. Vin Gris de Cigare: Grenache led, a true vin gris. Confirmed.
The cards and the questions: one right answer each. Sound.
The rules: the founder, the buyer and the winemaker are living and not named; no price; nothing volatile left in the making; British; no dash. Sound.

changed.was: The method has changed over the years. Older vintages were raised partly in puncheons of 500 litres and partly in large wooden uprights, some later ones partly in five gallon glass demijohns, and the 2023 in stainless steel tanks, bottled ten months after the harvest.
changed.now: The method has changed over the years. The 2012 and the 2015 were raised partly in puncheons and large wooden uprights, the 2015 in part also in five gallon glass demijohns, while a later release was aged in stainless steel tanks and bottled ten months after the harvest.
changed.why: The puncheons' size was not found, and the 2023 by name was a recent vintage report; the vessels are tied to the vintages the house's pages give.
